title: Update: You gave me feedback. I listened.
author: KimOnMacro
selftext:
For anyone seeing this for the first time: I'm improving an AI that automates your premarket prep (news, the institutional positioning, the macro values) and turns it into simple summary.   
  
  
**My goal is that even if you knew absolutely nothing about macroeconomics, institutional positioning or only ever traded with technical analysis etc, that it can still be understood simply, accurately, and applied to your trading to stack the probability in your favour.**   


Two weeks ago I posted here. I was genuinely happy lots of you are still using it and many messaged me after with feedback or what they thought. Some lovely proper roasts in there too 😂 but all genuinely useful as it gave me more ideas on how to make the user experience better!!   
  
Here's what common questions and thoughts came up, and what I did about each one.  


**How is this different from ChatGPT?** 

Bluntly, it's the architecture. This is plugged into paid, live data sources, at the expense of my own wallet (since commercial data licensing isn't cheap). An LLM on its own gives you a reasonable sounding answer built on whatever context it's holding, not live data.   
  
To make that difference visible instead of just claimed, I exposed the actual factors running in the loading animation, so you can see the filtered values and factors being cross checked when it does each run. I also rebuilt the UI as a flowchart instead of just bullet points, so it can communicate the reasoning visually much easier too!   


**Isn't it scary trusting AI? Is it accurate? Isn't COT data lagging data so why would you use it for day trading?** 

Absolutely. I would never just buy as AI said theres a bullish bias.   
  
The summary doesnt mean bullish so "enter now." It helps you interpret what just happened macro wise and what it means for your risk, weighing multiple factors together, not spitting out a signal.   
  
For example, with the same macro data, same news, you can try yourself on the app, but if you click the day toggle vs the swing toggle, oftentimes that diverges the macro bias where intraday might be bullish but swing might be bearish (Since swing weighs COT positioning and core macro data heavily, while intraday uses more finer price tickers, more recent news or upcoming economic prints instead.)  
  
Daytrading bias still uses COT however. Main reason why is that it can still flag traps. (e.g. price breaks a high, so you might think theres a breakout but if the COT report shows most of the institutions already bought, there's no one left to push momentum through = less chance of a real breakout etc.

To improve on this concern I weaved the explanation of the COT data into the main reasoning area on the dashboard so traps would be easily mentioned here. Also, made it so you dont have to go to the COT page, and you can just click the button to see where the institutions are at in terms of a week over week graph. 

  
**I saw some news that was released but didnt find it on the app!**

This was genuinely our filter being too strict! I made this much looser now, so it does catch more breaking sources even if sources may be from minor sites. Also allowed non-english sources as I've put on auto translation (So interestingly I get a lot of vietnamese news that comes out faster than american news for certain assets like btcusd lol). Still trying to find a sweet spot in terms of which news feeds everyone likes to listen to etc so up for ideas here.   
  
In the meantime, if you're after just fast feeds, you can check the Market Voices section, where I've added Financial Juice and Unusual Whales posts for breaking news. (although this is again through paid API so I have honestly kept it to **15-30 minute refreshes for now while we are in free beta**). If you need purely news speed, then they have free sites so would recommend to visit theirs if you havent used it already!   


**How I actually use this myself**

Simply put: I read the summary, check how long a bias is likely to hold (E.g any events that could change this?), then use technical analysis for final entry. If macro looks good but technicals dont, then I dont enter. If technicals look good but macro doesnt I dont enter. If they both match well then I enter.  
  
Before I built this though, my own process was:  
1) Start with macro values: Real yields and their spread, interest rate differentials, to see where money's actually flowing.  
2) Cross-check that against COT positioning so I'm not trading against the banks.   
3) Layer in news for context  
4) Then narrow to intraday signals, e.g. hourly vix etc  
5) Use technicals to enter.   


My app will automate step 1 through to 4, then I do my step 5 myself manually (TA).   
So basically I do 2 steps now. 

Anyways that was a super long post.  
  
If you haven't gotten bored yet and would love to help make EchelonEdgeAI a better experience I would genuinely appreciate that extra feedback!

Questions, confusion, "this part's useless," "I didnt understand" etc anything would be amazing guys! 

If you want to try it for free, drop a comment and I'll send it over!

comments.author: Interesting_Gold_792
comments.body: I really like that you’re focusing on explaining the reasoning instead of replacing the trader. One thing I’ve learned while building my own project is that trust doesn’t come from a higher win rate—it comes from helping users understand *why* the system believes something and *what would invalidate that belief*. I think showing changing confidence over time and exposing the evidence chain is a much stronger direction than another buy/sell signal. Curious how you’re thinking about handling conflicting signals instead of simply filtering them out.

replies.author: KimOnMacro
replies.body:
Appreciate that. That's pretty much the philosophy I've ended up with as well.  
One thing I deliberately avoid is filtering conflicting signals away, because the market itself is often conflicted. Instead, I try to weigh them based on timeframe and importance.

For example, strong macro and positioning might be bullish over the next few weeks, while today's news or an upcoming CPI release creates short-term downside risk. Rather than forcing a single answer, the app can end up with a bullish swing bias and a bearish intraday bias at the same time.  
  
The goal isn't to hide uncertainty but to explain *why* it exists and what would need to change for that view to flip. That's also why every verdict includes what could invalidate it. If the evidence changes, the bias should change too.

Still experimenting with how to communicate that visually though. I think that's one of the harder UX problems. As many new users often thought "Oh bias says this, therefore price action must be this etc"
